title: Why King Jehoiachin Ate at Another King’s Table for Years
paragraphs: Why King Jehoiachin Ate at Another King’s Table for Years
There are some people in Scripture whose stories feel unfinished.
They disappear into silence.

No grand comeback.
No dramatic victory speech.
No triumphant music playing behind them.

Just chains.
Just consequences.
Just years.
King Jehoiachin was one of them.
Most believers barely remember his name.
But buried inside the ashes of Jerusalem’s collapse is one of the most emotionally devastating and hope-filled stories in the entire Bible.
Because after decades in prison...

after humiliation...
after national disgrace...
after losing everything...
this fallen king spent the rest of his life eating at the table of another king.
And the reason why may reveal something terrifying and beautiful about judgment, mercy, exile, identity, and the kind of grace God gives to people who destroyed their own lives.
This is not merely political history.
This is the anatomy of restoration.
And if you have ever felt like you ruined your future through your own failures, this story will feel painfully personal.
Be honest.
Some of us know exactly what it feels like to sit inside consequences we created ourselves.
Some people reading this are carrying silent prisons nobody else can see.
And yet somehow… God still leaves room for mercy.
That is where Jehoiachin’s story begins.
The Boy King Who Inherited a Dying Kingdom
Jehoiachin became king of Judah at only eighteen years old.
Second Kings 24:8 says:
“Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months.”
Three months.
That was it.
Three months on a collapsing throne.

The kingdom of Judah was already spiritually rotting from generations of rebellion against God. Idolatry polluted the land. Corruption infected leadership. Prophets were ignored. Covenant warnings had been mocked for years.
The Babylonian Empire under King Nebuchadnezzar was rising like a storm God Himself allowed.
The Hebrew text repeatedly uses the covenant name:
יְהוָה — YHWH
The divine covenant name of God.

Not a distant force.
Not fate.
Not random history.
The destruction coming upon Judah was directly tied to covenant violation.
Second Kings 24:2 says:
“And YHWH sent against him bands of the Chaldeans…”
This matters deeply.
Because the exile was not simply geopolitical.
It was spiritual.
Judah did not merely lose wars.
Judah lost intimacy with God.
And Jehoiachin inherited the collapse.
Imagine being eighteen years old and sitting on a throne already covered in judgment.

No time to fix anything.
No time to rebuild.
No time to undo generations of rebellion.
Only incoming disaster.
Some people inherit blessings.
Others inherit ruins.
Jehoiachin inherited ruins.
The Meaning of His Name Makes the Story Even Sadder
The Hebrew name Jehoiachin is:
יְהוֹיָכִין — Yehoyakhin
It means:

“YHWH establishes”
or
“YHWH will uphold.”
Think about how heartbreaking that is.
A man named “God establishes” watches his kingdom collapse.
A man whose very identity points to divine stability loses everything.
Have you ever experienced that kind of contradiction?
You carry promises from God...
but your reality feels completely opposite.
You pray.
But things still fall apart.
You believed.
But life still shattered.
That tension lives all over Jehoiachin’s story.
And it still lives inside many believers today.
The Day Everything Ended
Second Kings 24 records the terrifying surrender.
Jehoiachin, his mother, his servants, officials, and palace leaders all surrendered to Babylon.
The Hebrew word often associated with exile is:
גָּלָה — galah
Meaning:

“To uncover.”
“To remove.”
“To carry away into captivity.”
Exile in Scripture is not merely relocation.
It is exposure.
Everything hidden gets uncovered.

Pride gets uncovered.
Sin gets uncovered.
False security gets uncovered.
Babylon stripped Judah of illusions.
Nebuchadnezzar carried Jehoiachin into captivity.
The king became a prisoner.
The royal bloodline sat in chains.
Second Kings 24:15 says:
“He carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon…”
The king who once sat above others now sat beneath another empire.
And then came the years.
Long years.
Silent years.
Forgotten years.
Imagine the psychological destruction.
Jehoiachin knew Jerusalem was devastated.
He knew the temple was under threat.
He knew his dynasty appeared cursed.
And every morning he woke up inside Babylon.
The same Babylon that symbolized rebellion against God all throughout Scripture.

The place of confusion.
The place of pride.
The place of spiritual captivity.
There are prisons made of iron.
And there are prisons made of regret.
Many people survive the first one.
The second one destroys them.
The Curse That Made His Story Look Hopeless
Then comes one of the darkest moments.
In Jeremiah 22:30, God declares concerning Jehoiachin:
“Write this man down as childless…”
The Hebrew phrase is deeply severe.
The judgment appears dynastic.
It sounds like the royal line is finished.
To ancient Israel, this was catastrophic.
Kingship in Judah was tied to the Davidic covenant.
God had promised David that his throne would endure.
Now Jehoiachin’s future looked erased.
Destroyed.
Finished.
There are moments where God’s discipline feels irreversible.
Moments where people think:
“I ruined everything.”
Maybe that is where some readers are right now.
You know what you did.
You know the damage.
You know the fallout.
And secretly you wonder whether restoration is even possible anymore.
Jehoiachin’s story sits inside that emotional darkness.
Which is exactly why what happens next becomes so shocking.
Thirty-Seven Years Later
Most people miss this.
Jehoiachin remained imprisoned for thirty-seven years.
Thirty-seven.

Not thirty-seven days.
Not thirty-seven months.
Thirty-seven years.
Second Kings 25:27 says:
“In the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah…”
Can you imagine the emotional weight of that sentence?

Thirty-seven years of wondering.
Thirty-seven years of remembering.
Thirty-seven years of shame.
Thirty-seven years of replaying failures.
Some people reading this have almost given up after three months.
Jehoiachin waited nearly four decades.
And then suddenly… everything changed.
Not because he fought his way out.
Not because he earned restoration.
Not because he rebuilt his reputation.
A new Babylonian king arose:
Evil-merodach.
In Akkadian, his name was likely tied to the Babylonian deity Marduk.
And this pagan king did something astonishing.
He lifted Jehoiachin from prison.
The Hebrew wording in Second Kings 25:27 is deeply emotional:
נָשָׂא אֶת־רֹאשׁ — nasa et-rosh
Literally:
“He lifted up the head.”
This phrase carries the idea of restoration of dignity.
Jehoiachin’s head had hung low for decades.
Now another king lifts it.
What an image.
Some of you have walked with your head down for years.

Years of shame.
Years of guilt.
Years of spiritual exhaustion.
Years of feeling disqualified.
And yet Scripture repeatedly reveals a God who still lifts heads.
Psalm 3:3 says:
“But You, O YHWH, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head.”
The Bible connects restoration with lifted heads.
God restores dignity to the humbled.
Not pride.
Dignity.
There is a difference.
Why Did Jehoiachin Eat at Another King’s Table?
Second Kings 25:29 says:
“So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments. And every day of his life he dined regularly at the king’s table.”
This is one of the most cinematic verses in Scripture.

A former prisoner.
A disgraced king.
A failed leader.
A man crushed by judgment.
Now sitting at the table of a foreign king.
Every day.
For the rest of his life.
Why?
Historically, ancient kings often used royal tables to symbolize covenant loyalty, political favor, protection, and ongoing provision.
But spiritually, the symbolism goes much deeper.
Jehoiachin becomes a living picture of mercy after judgment.
He did not regain the throne.
Notice that carefully.
This story is not cheap triumphalism.
God’s mercy did not erase consequences.

Jerusalem still fell.
The exile still happened.
The suffering was still real.
But mercy entered the story anyway.
That matters.
Because many believers wrongly think grace means pretending consequences never existed.
Biblical grace is deeper than denial.
Grace means God still feeds you even after your collapse.
Grace means God preserves you when you deserved destruction.
Grace means your failures do not get final authority over your identity.
Jehoiachin ate at another king’s table because mercy gave him what judgment alone did not.

Provision.
Protection.
Dignity.
Continuation.
And hidden inside this moment is an even bigger prophetic thread.
The Shocking Connection to Jesus Christ
This part changes everything.
Matthew 1 includes Jehoiachin in the genealogy of Jesus.

Even after exile.
Even after disgrace.
Even after judgment.
The line continued.
Matthew 1:11 says:
“Josiah begot Jeconiah and his brothers about the time they were carried away to Babylon.”
Jeconiah is another form of Jehoiachin’s name.
This means the Messiah’s earthly genealogy passed through exile.
Passed through humiliation.
Passed through apparent failure.
God did not erase the broken parts from the story.
He redeemed through them.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus Christ entered a human bloodline full of scandal, weakness, rebels, failures, outsiders, adulterers, and exiles.
Not because sin is acceptable.
But because redemption is real.
The Greek word for grace in the New Testament is:
χάρις — charis
Meaning:

Grace.
Favor.
Gift.
Unearned kindness.
Jehoiachin’s seat at the table was charis before the New Testament was ever written.
Mercy he did not deserve.
Favor he could not manufacture.
Provision he could never repay.
And the Gospel announces the same thing to us.
Many people think Christianity is about pretending to be flawless.
No.
Christianity is about sinners being invited to a King’s table.
Not because they are innocent.
Because Jesus is merciful.
Luke 22 becomes even more powerful through this lens.
Jesus sits with broken disciples at a table.

Men who will fail Him.
Men who will run.
Men who will deny Him.
And He still feeds them.
Still loves them.
Still calls them His own.
The Bible is filled with table imagery.
David writes in Psalm 23:
Tables in Scripture symbolize fellowship, covenant, provision, peace, acceptance, and relationship.
Jehoiachin’s prison garments were removed before he sat at the king’s table.
Do you see the imagery?
Prison garments removed.
A seat given.
Daily bread supplied.
That sounds astonishingly close to the Gospel.
The Part Most People Never Notice
The text says:
“Every day of his life.”
Not temporarily.
Not occasionally.
Continually.
Mercy sustained him daily.
This mirrors the heartbeat of biblical grace.
God’s mercy is not merely an emergency room visit.
It is daily bread.
Lamentations 3:22–23 says:
“His mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning.”
Some believers think God barely tolerates them.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals God sustaining broken people day after day.
Not because He ignores sin.
But because His mercy is greater than despair.
And somebody reading this desperately needs to hear that.
You are not beyond redemption.
You are not too shattered.
You are not too late.
You are not too stained for grace.
Jehoiachin’s story survived in Scripture because God wanted future generations to know that exile does not always get the final word.
Babylon Was Not His Final Identity
This may be the deepest lesson of all.
Jehoiachin lived in Babylon.
But Babylon no longer defined him.
He was sustained at the king’s table.
The enemy that once held him captive became the place where unexpected mercy appeared.
Some believers are currently in seasons that feel like Babylon.

Grief.
Depression.
Failure.
Addiction.
Divorce.
Spiritual exhaustion.
Loneliness.
Consequences.
But your current location is not necessarily your eternal identity.
Exile is painful.
But God still works inside exile.
Even there.
Especially there.
Some people need to know they are not alone in their struggle.
Some people are surviving externally while collapsing internally.
Because sometimes the people sitting quietly at the table carry stories of prisons nobody else survived.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Kumain si Haring Jehoiachin sa Mesa ng Ibang Hari sa Loob ng Napakaraming Taon
May mga tao sa Kasulatan na parang hindi natapos ang kuwento.
Bigla na lang silang nawawala sa katahimikan.
Walang engrandeng pagbabalik. Walang matagumpay na talumpati. Walang tunog ng tagumpay sa likuran.
Kadena lang. Mga bunga ng kasalanan. Mahahabang taon.
Isa si Haring Jehoiachin sa kanila.
Karamihan sa mga mananampalataya halos hindi na siya maalala.
Pero nakabaon sa abo ng pagbagsak ng Jerusalem ang isa sa pinakamabigat at pinaka-punong-pag-asa na kuwento sa buong Bibliya.
Dahil matapos ang mga dekada sa bilangguan...
matapos ang kahihiyan... matapos mawala ang lahat... matapos durugin ang kaniyang pangalan...
ang bagsak na haring ito ay kumain sa mesa ng ibang hari habang siya’y nabubuhay.

At ang dahilan kung bakit maaaring magbunyag ng isang napakalalim na katotohanan tungkol sa paghatol, awa, pagkabihag, identidad, at biyayang ibinibigay ng Diyos sa mga taong sumira ng sarili nilang buhay.
Hindi lang ito simpleng kasaysayan.
Ito ang anatomya ng restorasyon.
At kung naramdaman mo nang sinira mo mismo ang sarili mong kinabukasan dahil sa mga maling desisyon mo, tatagos ito nang malalim.
Maging totoo tayo.
May mga tao ritong nakakulong sa mga bunga ng sarili nilang ginawa.
May mga nakakulong sa lihim na piitan na walang ibang nakakakita.
At kahit ganoon… may puwang pa rin ang awa ng Diyos.
Diyan nagsisimula ang kuwento ni Jehoiachin.
Ang Batang Haring Umupo sa Gumuguhong Kaharian
Naging hari si Jehoiachin sa edad na labing-walo.
Sinasabi ng 2 Hari 24:8:
“Si Jehoiachin ay labing walong taong gulang nang siya’y magpasimulang maghari sa Jerusalem at siya’y nagharing tatlong buwan.”
Tatlong buwan.
Iyon lang.
Tatlong buwan sa isang trono na halos wasak na.

Ang Juda noon ay bulok na espirituwal dahil sa paulit-ulit na pagrerebelde laban sa Diyos. Kumalat ang idolatriya. Naging normal ang kasamaan. Hindi pinakinggan ang mga propeta. Minamaliit ang mga babala ng tipan ng Diyos.
At habang lumalalim ang kasalanan ng Juda, lumalakas naman ang Babilonia sa ilalim ni Haring Nebuchadnezzar.
Paulit-ulit na ginagamit sa Hebreo ang pangalan ng Diyos:
יְהוָה — YHWH
Ito ang banal na pangalan ng Diyos ng tipan.
Hindi aksidente ang pagbagsak. Hindi ito simpleng pulitika.
Direktang konektado ang paghatol sa paglabag ng bayan sa Diyos.
Sinasabi ng 2 Hari 24:2:
“At nagsugo si YHWH laban sa kaniya ng mga hukbo ng mga Caldeo…”
Napakahalaga nito.
Dahil hindi lang digmaan ang nawala sa Juda.
Nawala nila ang malapit na relasyon sa Diyos.
At si Jehoiachin ang umupo sa gitna ng pagbagsak.
Isipin mong labing-walong taong gulang ka pa lang pero nakaupo ka na sa trono ng paghuhukom.
Wala nang oras para ayusin. Wala nang oras para bumawi. Wala nang oras para itama ang kasalanan ng mga naunang henerasyon.
Paparating na ang pagkawasak.
May mga taong namamana ang pagpapala.
May mga taong namamana ang guho.
Namana ni Jehoiachin ang guho.
Mas Masakit Kapag Naunawaan Mo ang Kahulugan ng Pangalan Niya
Sa Hebreo, ang Jehoiachin ay:
יְהוֹיָכִין — Yehoyakhin
Ang ibig sabihin:
“Si YHWH ang magtatatag.” o “Si YHWH ang magpapatibay.”
Napakasakit isipin.
Isang lalaking ang pangalan ay “itatatag ng Diyos” pero nawalan ng kaharian.
Isang lalaking ang identidad ay konektado sa katatagan ng Diyos pero nakita niyang bumagsak ang lahat.
Naranasan mo na ba iyon?
May mga pangako ang Diyos sa iyo...
pero parang kabaligtaran ang nangyayari sa buhay mo.
Nananalangin ka.
Pero parang lalong nagugulo.
Naniwala ka.
Pero parang nawasak pa rin.
Iyan ang tensyon sa kuwento ni Jehoiachin.
At iyan pa rin ang tensyon ng maraming Kristiyano ngayon.
Ang Araw na Nawasak ang Lahat
Inilarawan sa 2 Hari 24 ang nakakatakot na pagsuko.
Si Jehoiachin, ang kaniyang ina, mga lingkod, opisyal, at mga pinuno ay sumuko sa Babilonia.
Isa sa mga salitang Hebreo para sa pagkabihag ay:
גָּלָה — galah
Ang ibig sabihin:
“Ilantad.” “Alisin.” “Dalhin sa pagkabihag.”
Sa Bibliya, ang exile ay hindi lang paglilipat ng lugar.
Ito ay paglalantad.
Nalalantad ang pagmamataas. Nalalantad ang kasalanan. Nalalantad ang maling seguridad.
Hinubaran ng Babilonia ang Juda ng ilusyon.
Dinala si Jehoiachin bilang bihag.
Ang hari ay naging bilanggo.
Sinasabi ng 2 Hari 24:15:
“Dinala niya si Jehoiachin sa Babilonia…”
Ang dating nakaupo sa trono ay nakaupo na ngayon sa kulungan.
At pagkatapos noon… dumating ang mahabang mga taon.
Tahimik na mga taon. Nakakalimutang mga taon. Masasakit na mga taon.
Isipin mo ang emosyonal na pagkawasak.
Alam ni Jehoiachin na wasak ang Jerusalem.
Alam niyang nasa bingit ang templo.
Alam niyang parang isinumpa na ang kanilang linya.
At bawat umaga, nagigising siya sa Babilonia.
Ang Babilonia na simbolo ng pagmamataas at pagrerebelde laban sa Diyos.
May mga piitang bakal.
At may mga piitang gawa sa pagsisisi.
Mas maraming tao ang nasisira sa pangalawa.
Ang Sumpang Nagmukhang Katapusan ng Lahat
Sa Jeremias 22:30, sinabi ng Diyos tungkol kay Jehoiachin:
“Isulat ninyo ang taong ito na parang walang anak…”
Napakabigat ng paghatol.
Parang tapos na ang kanilang linya.
Sa Israel noon, napakalaking bagay nito.
Dahil konektado ang trono sa tipan ng Diyos kay David.
Nangako ang Diyos na magpapatuloy ang linya ni David.
Pero ngayon parang nabura na ang kinabukasan ni Jehoiachin.
Ganito rin minsan ang pakiramdam ng maraming tao.
“Sinira ko na lahat.”
Baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na alam ang bigat ng sariling kasalanan.
Alam mo ang ginawa mo.
Alam mo ang nasaktan.
At lihim mong iniisip kung posible pa bang maibalik ng Diyos ang anumang nawasak.
Diyan naging pinakamadilim ang kuwento ni Jehoiachin.
At dahil doon, lalong naging makapangyarihan ang susunod na mangyayari.
Tatlumpu’t Pitong Taon ang Lumipas
Ito ang hindi napapansin ng karamihan.
Tatlumpo’t pitong taon nakakulong si Jehoiachin.
Hindi tatlumpu’t pitong araw. Hindi tatlumpu’t pitong buwan.
Tatlumpu’t pitong taon.
Sinasabi ng 2 Hari 25:27:
“Nang ikatatlumpu’t pitong taon ng pagkabihag ni Jehoiachin…”
Napakabigat ng linyang iyon.
Tatlumpu’t pitong taon ng pag-iisip. Tatlumpu’t pitong taon ng kahihiyan. Tatlumpu’t pitong taon ng pagsisisi. Tatlumpu’t pitong taon ng pag-alala sa pagkakamali.
May mga taong halos sumuko na pagkatapos ng ilang buwan.
Si Jehoiachin naghintay ng halos apat na dekada.
At pagkatapos… biglang nagbago ang lahat.
Hindi dahil pinaglaban niya ang sarili niya.
Hindi dahil binawi niya ang reputasyon niya.
Hindi dahil karapat-dapat siya.
Isang bagong hari ng Babilonia ang dumating.
Si Evil-merodach.
At gumawa siya ng isang nakakagulat na bagay.
Pinalaya niya si Jehoiachin.
Sa Hebreo, ang ginamit na salita ay:
נָשָׂא אֶת־רֹאשׁ — nasa et-rosh
Literal na ibig sabihin:
“Itinaas niya ang ulo.”
Larawan ito ng pagbabalik ng dignidad.
Matagal nakayuko ang ulo ni Jehoiachin.
Pero itinaas iyon ng isang hari.
Napakalalim na larawan.
May mga taong ilang taon nang nakayuko.
Dahil sa kahihiyan. Dahil sa pagkakasala. Dahil sa depresyon. Dahil sa pakiramdam na wala nang pag-asa.
Pero paulit-ulit na ipinapakita ng Kasulatan na ang Diyos ay nagtataas pa rin ng mga ulo.
Sinasabi ng Awit 3:3:
“Ikaw, O YHWH, ang tagapagtaas ng aking ulo.”
Hindi pinapalakas ng Diyos ang pagmamataas.
Ibinabalik Niya ang dignidad.
Bakit Siya Kumain sa Mesa ng Ibang Hari?
Sinasabi ng 2 Hari 25:29:
“Hinubad ni Jehoiachin ang kaniyang kasuotang bilanggo at araw-araw siyang kumakain sa hapag ng hari habang siya’y nabubuhay.”
Napakagandang eksena nito sa Bibliya.
Isang dating bilanggo. Isang bagsak na hari. Isang taong dinurog ng paghatol.
Ngayon nakaupo sa mesa ng ibang hari.
Araw-araw.
Habang siya’y nabubuhay.
Bakit?
Noong unang panahon, ang pagkain sa mesa ng hari ay simbolo ng proteksiyon, pabor, tipan, at patuloy na pagtanggap.
Pero mas malalim pa rito ang espirituwal na kahulugan.
Si Jehoiachin ay naging buhay na larawan ng awa matapos ang paghatol.
Hindi naibalik ang trono niya.
Pansinin mo iyon.
Hindi binura ng awa ng Diyos ang lahat ng consequences.
Bumagsak pa rin ang Jerusalem. Nangyari pa rin ang exile. Totoo pa rin ang sakit.
Pero pumasok pa rin ang awa.
Napakahalaga niyan.
Maraming tao ang iniisip na ang biyaya ay parang pagkunwari na walang nangyaring kasalanan.
Hindi.
Mas malalim ang biyaya.
Ang biyaya ay pinapakain ka pa rin ng Diyos kahit bumagsak ka.
Ang biyaya ay hindi hinahayaang ang kabiguan mo ang maging huling salita tungkol sa pagkatao mo.
Kumain si Jehoiachin sa mesa ng ibang hari dahil may awa pa rin matapos ang paghatol.
May pagkain. May proteksiyon. May dignidad. May pagpapatuloy.
At may mas malaking propetikong larawan dito.
Ang Nakakagulat na Koneksiyon Kay Jesucristo
Dito lalong lumalalim ang kuwento.
Kasama si Jehoiachin sa genealogy ni Jesus sa Mateo 1.
Kahit may exile. Kahit may kahihiyan. Kahit may paghatol.
Nagpatuloy pa rin ang linya.
Sinasabi ng Mateo 1:11:
“Si Josias ang ama ni Jeconias…”
Si Jeconias ay ibang anyo ng pangalang Jehoiachin.
Ibig sabihin, dumaan ang genealogy ng Mesiyas sa kahihiyan at pagkabihag.
Hindi binura ng Diyos ang mga sirang bahagi ng kuwento.
Tinubos Niya ang mga ito.
Iyan ang Ebanghelyo.
Pumasok si Jesucristo sa linya ng mga makasalanan, sugatan, bagsak, at sirang tao.
Hindi dahil okay lang ang kasalanan.
Kundi dahil totoo ang pagtubos.
Sa Griyego, ang salitang biyaya ay:
χάρις — charis
Ibig sabihin:
Biyaya. Pabor. Hindi karapat-dapat na kabutihan.
Ang upuan ni Jehoiachin sa mesa ng hari ay larawan ng charis bago pa naisulat ang Bagong Tipan.
Awa na hindi niya kayang kitain.
Pabor na hindi niya kayang bayaran.
At ganoon din ang Ebanghelyo.
Hindi tungkol sa pagpapanggap na perpekto ang Kristiyanismo.
Ito ay tungkol sa mga makasalanan na inaanyayahang umupo sa mesa ng Hari.
Hindi dahil inosente sila.
Kundi dahil maawain si Jesus.
Ang Bahaging Hindi Napapansin ng Marami
Sinasabi ng teksto:
“Araw-araw habang siya’y nabubuhay.”
Hindi pansamantala.
Hindi paminsan-minsan.
Araw-araw.
Ganiyan ang biyaya ng Diyos.
Hindi lang ito pang-emergency.
Ito ay araw-araw na habag.
Sinasabi ng Panaghoy 3:22–23:
“Bago tuwing umaga ang Kaniyang mga habag.”
May mga Kristiyanong pakiramdam nila barely silang tinitiis ng Diyos.
Pero paulit-ulit na ipinapakita ng Kasulatan na patuloy na inaalagaan ng Diyos ang mga taong sugatan.
Hindi dahil walang kasalanan.
Kundi dahil mas dakila ang awa Niya kaysa sa desperasyon natin.
At baka may nagbabasa nito ngayon na kailangang marinig iyon.
Hindi ka pa huli.
Hindi ka pa tapos.
Hindi ka masyadong marumi para sa biyaya ng Diyos.
Hindi masyadong malalim ang pagkabagsak mo para abutin ka ni Cristo.
Hindi Babilonia ang Huling Pagkakakilanlan Niya
Ito marahil ang pinakamalalim na aral.
Nasa Babilonia si Jehoiachin.
Pero hindi na Babilonia ang nagbigay ng huling identidad niya.
Dahil pinapakain siya sa mesa ng hari.
Ang lugar ng pagkabihag niya ay naging lugar din ng hindi inaasahang awa.
May mga tao ritong nasa sarili nilang “Babilonia.”
Kalungkutan. Depresyon. Pagkabigo. Pagkagumon. Pagkapagod. Pag-iisa. Mga consequences.
Pero ang kasalukuyan mong lokasyon ay hindi awtomatikong iyong eternal na identidad.
Masakit ang exile.
Pero kumikilos pa rin ang Diyos kahit sa exile.
Kahit doon.
Lalo na doon.
May mga taong kailangang malaman na hindi sila nag-iisa.
